The '''Borel distribution''' is a [[discrete probability distribution]], arising in contexts including [[branching process]]es and [[queueing theory]]. It is named after the French mathematician [[Émile Borel]].

If the number of offspring that an organism has is [[Poisson distribution|Poisson-distributed]], and if the average number of offspring of each organism is no bigger than&nbsp;1, then the descendants of each individual will ultimately become extinct.  The number of descendants that an individual ultimately has in that situation is a random variable distributed according to a Borel distribution.

==Definition==
A discrete [[random variable]] ''X{{space}}'' is said to have a Borel distribution<ref>{{cite journal | first = Émile | last = Borel | author-link = Émile Borel | title = Sur l'emploi du théorème de Bernoulli pour faciliter le calcul d'une infinité de coefficients. Application au problème de l'attente à un guichet. | journal = [[C. R. Acad. Sci.]] | volume = 214 | pages = 452–456 | year = 1942}}</ref><ref name="Tanner1961">{{Cite journal | last1 = Tanner | first1 = J. C. | doi = 10.1093/biomet/48.1-2.222 | title = A derivation of the Borel distribution | journal = [[Biometrika]]| volume = 48 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 222–224 | year = 1961 | jstor = 2333154}}</ref>
with parameter ''μ''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;[0,1] if the [[probability mass function]] of ''X'' is given by

:<math>P_\mu(n)= \Pr(X=n)= \frac{e^{-\mu n}(\mu n)^{n-1}}{n!}</math>

for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;3&nbsp;....

==Derivation and branching process interpretation==
If a [[branching process|Galton–Watson branching process]] has common offspring distribution [[Poisson distribution|Poisson]] with mean ''μ'', then the total number of individuals in the branching process has Borel distribution with parameter&nbsp;''μ''.

Let ''X{{space}}'' be the total number of individuals in a Galton–Watson branching process. 
Then a correspondence between the total size of the branching process and a hitting time for an associated [[random walk]]<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Otter | first1 = R. | title = The Multiplicative Process | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177730031 | journal = The Annals of Mathematical Statistics | volume = 20 | issue = 2 | pages = 206–224 | year = 1949 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Dwass>{{cite journal | last1 = Dwass | first1 = Meyer  | year = 1969 | title = The Total Progeny in a Branching Process and a Related Random Walk | journal = Journal of Applied Probability | volume = 6 | issue = 3 | pages = 682–686 | jstor = 3212112 | doi = 10.2307/3212112  }}</ref><ref name=Pitman>{{cite journal | first = Jim | last =Pitman
| title = Enumerations Of Trees And Forests Related To Branching Processes And Random Walks | year = 1997
| journal = Microsurveys in Discrete Probability: DIMACS Workshop | number = 41 | 
url = http://statistics.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/tech-reports/482.pdf}}
</ref> gives

: <math>\Pr(X=n)=\frac{1}{n}\Pr(S_n=n-1)</math>

where ''S''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''Y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;…&nbsp;+&nbsp;''Y''<sub>''n''</sub>, and ''Y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;…&nbsp;''Y''<sub>''n''</sub> are [[independent identically distributed random variables]] whose common distribution is the offspring distribution of the branching process. 
In the case where this common distribution is Poisson with mean ''μ'', the random variable
''S''<sub>''n''</sub> has Poisson distribution with mean ''μn'',
leading to the mass function of the Borel distribution given above.

Since the ''m''th generation of the branching process has mean size ''μ''<sup>''m''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1</sup>,
the mean of ''X{{space}}'' is

: <math>1+\mu+\mu^2+\cdots = \frac 1 {1-\mu}.</math>

==Queueing theory interpretation==
In an [[M/D/1 queue]] with arrival rate ''μ'' and common service time 1, 
the distribution of a typical busy period of the queue is Borel with parameter ''μ''.
<ref name=HaightBreuer>{{Cite journal | last1 = Haight | first1 = F. A. | last2 = Breuer | first2 = M. A. | doi = 10.1093/biomet/47.1-2.143 | title = The Borel-Tanner distribution | journal = [[Biometrika]]| volume = 47 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 143–150 | year = 1960 | jstor = 2332966}}</ref>

==Properties==
If ''P''<sub>''μ''</sub>(''n'') is the probability mass function of a 
Borel(''μ'') random variable, then the mass function
''P''{{su|p=&lowast;|b=''&mu;''}}(''n'')
of a sized-biased sample from the distribution 
(i.e. the mass function proportional to ''nP''<sub>''&mu;''</sub>(''n'')&nbsp;)
is given by

:<math>P_\mu^*(n)=(1-\mu)\frac{e^{-\mu n}(\mu n)^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}.</math>

Aldous and Pitman 
<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Aldous | first1 = D.| last2 = Pitman | first2 = J.| title = Tree-valued Markov chains derived from Galton-Watson processes | doi = 10.1016/S0246-0203(98)80003-4 | journal = Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré B | volume = 34 | issue = 5 | page = 637 | url = http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~pitman/481.pdf| year = 1998 | bibcode = 1998AIHPB..34..637A}}</ref>
show that

: <math>P_\mu(n)=\frac{1}{\mu} \int_0^\mu P_\lambda^*(n) \, d\lambda.</math>

In words, this says that a Borel(''μ'') random variable has the same distribution
as a size-biased Borel(''μU'') random variable, where ''U'' has the uniform distribution on&nbsp;[0,1].

This relation leads to various useful formulas, including

: <math>\operatorname E\left( \frac 1 X \right) = 1 - \frac \mu 2.</math>

==Borel–Tanner distribution==
The '''Borel–Tanner distribution''' generalizes the Borel distribution.
Let ''k'' be a positive integer. 
If ''X''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''X''<sub>2</sub>, &nbsp;…&nbsp;''X''<sub>''k''</sub>
are independent and each has
Borel distribution with parameter ''μ'', then their sum 
''W''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''X''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''X''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;…&nbsp;+&nbsp;''X''<sub>''k''</sub> is said to have Borel–Tanner distribution with parameters ''μ'' and ''k''.
<ref name="Tanner1961" /><ref name=HaightBreuer /><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Tanner | first1 = J. C. | doi = 10.1093/biomet/40.1-2.58 | title = A Problem of Interference Between Two Queues | journal = Biometrika | volume = 40 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 58–69 | year = 1953 | jstor = 2333097}}</ref>
This gives the distribution of the total number of individuals
in a Poisson–Galton–Watson process starting with ''k'' individuals in the first generation,
or of the time taken for an M/D/1 queue to empty starting with ''k'' jobs in the queue. 
The case ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 is simply the Borel distribution above.

Generalizing the random walk correspondence given above for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,<ref name=Dwass /><ref name=Pitman />

: <math>\Pr(W=n)= \frac k n \Pr(S_n=n-k)</math>

where ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> has Poisson distribution with mean ''nμ''.
As a result, the probability mass function is given by

: <math> \Pr(W=n)=\frac k n \frac{e^{-\mu n}(\mu n)^{n-k}}{(n-k)!} </math>

for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''k'',&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1,&nbsp;...&nbsp;.
